name: Harmony ratios

card.summary: Facial proportion measurements, such as eye spacing and eye-to-mouth distance relative to face size, that looksmaxxers compare against ideal values to decide which features to improve.
card.aka: facial ratios; golden ratio face analysis
card.note: Researchers dispute that fixed ideal ratios predict attractiveness; communities describe the system as imperfect.

quick.overview:
Harmony ratios are the proportions between facial features (for example the distance between the eyes versus face width, or eye-to-mouth distance versus face length) that looksmaxxers use as a yardstick of facial balance. People measure their own face, compare it against 'ideal' values or ethnic-specific reference faces, and use the gaps to choose what to work on, from hairstyle and glasses to procedures.

Research exists on facial proportions and attractiveness. A 2010 study found that preferred ratios clustered around the average of the faces tested (about 0.36 for length and 0.46 for width) and differed from the classical golden ratio. Forum users themselves describe ratio systems as flawed estimates.
quick.how: Users take front-facing photos, mark landmarks, compute ratios and compare them with tables of 'ideal' figures or with reference faces. The results feed decisions about grooming, hair, makeup, fillers or surgery, and forum users discuss them alongside symmetry and feature quality.
quick.risks: There is no physical risk from measuring, but ratio-based self-rating can anchor people to numbers that research does not treat as fixed targets. Photo angle and lens distortion change the measurements.

lead: Harmony ratios is the looksmaxxing term for the proportional relationships between facial features, such as eye spacing relative to face width and the vertical thirds of the face. Forum users treat 'harmony' as the way features balance together, often estimated through ratios and symmetry. [1]

The idea helps people improve their looks by turning a vague impression into measurable gaps. A user who finds a long midface or wide-set eyes might choose glasses, a hairstyle, makeup, fillers or surgery accordingly.

Scientific work on proportions includes a 2010 study by Pallett, Link and Lee, which tested edited faces and reported preferred ratios close to the average of the faces measured rather than to the classical 1.618 golden ratio. [3]

chain: Compare to ideal or average reference values
Pick grooming, cosmetic or surgical changes that shift the proportions
angle.text: Ratios are an analysis tool: they identify which proportions differ from a reference and so where changes such as hairstyle, makeup, filler or surgery might matter. The ratios themselves change nothing.

infobox: Interocular distance vs face width; eye-to-mouth distance vs face length

paras: Harmony analysis uses landmark-based measurements on a frontal photo. Common figures include the width of the face compared with the distance between the eyes, and the distance from eyes to mouth compared with face length. Forum users describe them as a quantification of how well features fit together, and some add that beauty cannot be fully quantified. [1]

Proportional ideals for the face descend from classical art and from the golden ratio, a number around 1.618. Looksmaxxing forums adapted these into ratio sheets and 'chad morph' references that vary by ethnicity, and use the vocabulary in rating threads. [1]

One looksmax.org post argues that conventionally attractive people share similar proportions and that AI-generated attractive faces converge on the same ratios, while still calling the system flawed. [1] Another thread jokes about which parent one inherits ratios from, with replies noting that genetics are not that simple. [2]

In the 2010 Pallett study, participants judged edited photos of Caucasian female faces. Attractiveness peaked at about 0.36 for the eye-to-mouth to face-length ratio and 0.46 for the interocular to face-width ratio, matching the averages of the 40 faces measured. [3] The authors said these differed from ratios based on the classical golden section. [3]
The authors listed limits: only Caucasian female faces, a small set of 40 faces for the average, and modest model fit for width. [3]
No studies found of harmony ratios as a looksmaxxing framework. Perceptual research on facial proportions, such as the 2010 study above, is described in the research section. [3]

timeline.event: Pallett, Link and Lee publish preferred facial length and width ratios in Vision Research. [3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, harmony and ratios are discussed as measurable parts of facial attractiveness, with frequent debate about how objective they are. [1]

claims.claim: Ideal ratios exist and conventionally attractive people share them
claims.believers: Proponents argue attractive faces across races show similar proportions and that comparing yourself to ethnic reference faces estimates your baseline. [1]
claims.experts: A 2010 study found preferred ratios near the average of the faces tested, not the classical golden ratio, in a limited sample. [3]

claims.claim: Harmony is inherited from a parent
claims.believers: Users trade jokes and anecdotes about inheriting ratios from one parent. [2]
claims.experts: No published study has examined inheritance of facial 'harmony' as defined in these threads.
